dmaic.intro: DMAIC is the core methodology of Six Sigma — a structured, data-driven approach for the sustainable improvement of existing processes. Its five phases Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve and Control lead you systematically from a vaguely perceived problem to a proven, permanently anchored solution.
dmaic.whyBody: Many improvement projects fail because they jump to a solution too early. DMAIC enforces discipline: first understand, then measure, then analyse — only then change. Decisions rest on data rather than opinions, and success is proven quantitatively at the end. That makes the methodology robust against gut-feel fixes and creates a transparent thread the whole project team can follow.
dmaic.defineBody: In the Define phase you clarify what the project is really about: which problem shall be solved, for whom, by when, and how will benefit and success be measured? Typical tools are the Project Charter with measurable goals (Goal Achievement Level, GAL), a coarse SIPOC to scope the process, a stakeholder analysis, and VOC/CTQ to translate customer voice into critical quality characteristics. The output is a tightly scoped project charter that everyone involved can agree on.
dmaic.measureBody: Before you improve, you need to know where you stand. The Measure phase delivers reliable data: a clean process description (process map), a trustworthy measurement method (MSA Type 1, Gage R&R) and baseline indicators for capability (Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk) and stability. Without a validated measurement system later improvements can neither be detected nor proven — which is why a sound measurement system is the central prerequisite for everything that follows.
dmaic.analyzeBody: Now you search systematically for the true root causes — not the symptoms. Ishikawa and 5-Why structure the thinking, correlation and hypothesis tests (t-test, ANOVA, Chi², regression) verify which suspected drivers are actually statistically significant. At the end of this phase you know the few critical X that really drive the Y of your process.
dmaic.improveBody: With the root-cause knowledge from Analyze you develop solutions and test them — ideally via a Design of Experiments (DOE) that varies multiple factors systematically at once. This reveals the best factor combination with evidence, quantifies interactions and avoids expensive one-factor-at-a-time trials. Pilot runs confirm the effect under real conditions before the change goes into the production process.
dmaic.controlBody: The best improvement evaporates without control. In Control you introduce control charts (SPC), update work instructions, assign responsibilities and define a reaction plan for deviations. At the end of this phase the project's success is verified against the goals agreed in Define, recorded in a Lessons-Learned document and formally handed over to the process owner.
dmaic.whenTitle: When is DMAIC the right tool?
dmaic.whenBody: DMAIC is particularly suited to existing processes with measurable performance whose causes for deviation are unclear. For new designs, DMADV (Design for Six Sigma) is more appropriate, and for quick wins Kaizen or PDCA. A DMAIC project is worth it when the problem is economically significant, the causes are unclear, and data is fundamentally available (or obtainable).
dmaic.pitfall1: Jumping to a solution too early — without an understood root cause it stays symptom fighting, and the problem comes back.
dmaic.pitfall2: Skipping the measurement system. If the measurement itself adds 30 % variation, every baseline number is unreliable.
dmaic.pitfall3: Scoping too broadly. A tightly bounded project scope beats an ambitious "fix everything" project every time.
dmaic.pitfall4: Neglecting the Control phase. Without control mechanisms and clear ownership the process drifts back within a few months.
dmaic.appBody: The header shows six phase tiles (Data, D, M, A, I, C). Each phase is a container into which you add the matching modules (Project Charter, SIPOC, MSA, Process Capability, Hypothesis Tests, DOE, Control Charts, Lessons Learned …) via the hamburger menu (☰) on each tile. That way your project grows step by step along the methodology — and can be exported to JSON, archived and re-imported at any time.

dmadv.intro: DMADV stands for Define · Measure · Analyze · Design · Verify and is the Design-for-Six-Sigma variant of the improvement cycle. Instead of fixing an existing process, DMADV helps you design a new process or product from scratch so it meets the required quality characteristics reliably and reproducibly.
dmadv.whyBody: DMAIC works beautifully when a process is already running and just needs to be optimised. For greenfield development — a new product, a new service line, a new manufacturing step — the baseline data DMAIC relies on is missing. DMADV replaces "improving" with systematic "designing": first the customer needs and critical-to-quality characteristics are captured, then the design is selected from data-driven alternatives, and finally it is verified that the design meets the spec under realistic conditions.
dmadv.defineTitle: Define — Sharpen the charter and customer requirements
dmadv.defineBody: As in DMAIC, DMADV starts with a clear project charter: what is to be built, for whom, with what business benefit, by when? But the customer focus is stronger — Voice of the Customer (VOC), stakeholder analysis and an initial requirements brief. By the end of the phase you have a charter that pins down development scope and success criteria from both customer and business perspectives.
dmadv.measureBody: This phase translates the customer needs from Define into measurable critical-to-quality characteristics (CTQs). Which properties must the finished product or new process exhibit? Which tolerances are acceptable, which minimum performance is non-negotiable? If reference data from similar processes is available, measurement systems are evaluated (MSA) and baseline metrics captured — they later serve as the comparison basis for the Verify phase.
dmadv.analyzeBody: DMADV-Analyze differs significantly from DMAIC-Analyze: instead of hunting for root causes, several design concepts are systematically compared. Pugh matrices, concept scoring, concept-level FMEA, statistical predictions and (where appropriate) simulations help you select the most promising concept. Hypothesis tests and correlations can already be used here to validate assumptions about how the future system will behave.
dmadv.designTitle: Design — Work the chosen concept out in detail
dmadv.designBody: The concept selected in Analyze is fleshed out into a concrete, technically detailed design. Factor designs (DOE) help identify critical control parameters and their optimal settings, regression builds prediction models for the key metrics, detailed-level FMEA surfaces remaining risks. Pilot builds or prototypes deliver the first hard data with which the design is iteratively optimised before the final verification.
dmadv.verifyTitle: Verify — Confirm the design in practice
dmadv.verifyBody: Verify is the DMADV equivalent of DMAIC-Control: the finished design is tested under real or near-production conditions. Process capability analyses (Cp, Cpk), control charts and hypothesis tests check whether the CTQs agreed in Define are actually met. Once the spec is reached, the design moves into series production / steady-state operation together with the lessons-learned, work instructions and reaction plan.
dmadv.whenTitle: When is DMADV the right tool?
dmadv.whenBody: DMADV fits when something new is to be created: a new product, a new service, a new manufacturing process or a fundamentally re-thought variant of an existing process. Even when an existing process has been improved to the point where further DMAIC iterations yield diminishing returns, DMADV can be the next logical step to redesign the process from the ground up. For correcting a running process, however, DMAIC remains the more efficient choice.
dmadv.pitfall1: Filling Define with solution descriptions instead of requirements — the design gets unconsciously narrowed to a predetermined solution before alternatives have even been examined.
dmadv.pitfall2: Skipping VOC and CTQs or formulating them only qualitatively. Without measurable target values, Verify lacks the yardstick against which the design can be judged.
dmadv.pitfall3: Jumping into detailed design too early, before Analyze has fairly compared multiple concepts — you save weeks now and pay months later.
dmadv.pitfall4: Treating Verify as a mere formality. If you don't test the design under realistic conditions, you hand risks over to operations that come back later as "unexplained" quality problems.
dmadv.appBody: When you create a project with the "DMADV" cycle, the header shows seven tiles (Data, D, M, A, D, V, More). Modules like SIPOC, FMEA, MSA or Hypothesis Tests are mapped to the matching phases automatically; DOE and regression live in the Design phase, control charts and lessons-learned in Verify. Tools without a fixed DMADV mapping appear in the right "More" tile and can be drag-and-dropped into a phase — full access to the entire toolkit is preserved.

eightd.intro: The 8D cycle (Eight Disciplines) is a structured problem-solving process for reactive defect resolution — typically triggered by a customer complaint, a recurring production defect or a safety incident. Across eight disciplines (nine when counting D0) it walks the team from immediate containment through root-cause analysis to durable prevention and finally formal recognition of the team.
eightd.whyBody: When a problem turns acute — complaint, line stop, recall — there isn't time for a multi-month DMAIC project. A quick fix alone won't do either: customers, auditors and your own quality system demand evidence that the problem is understood, durably fixed and prevented going forward. 8D delivers exactly that framework — short enough for real-world response times, thorough enough for a genuine root-cause investigation, and documented enough for a formal 8D report to the customer.
eightd.prepareBody: Before the team is formed, D0 settles the entry criteria: is this an 8D case (recurring defect, safety issue, customer complaint) or a routine deviation? Emergency Response Actions to contain immediate harm are documented here. D0 ends with a decision on whether 8D is the right process at all — and which initial safeguards take effect immediately.
eightd.teamBody: 8D is teamwork: you need representatives of every function that can understand, contain or durably resolve the problem — production, quality, engineering, supplier, service. Define champion, team leader, core team and extended team; clarify responsibilities (RACI); and make sure the team has the necessary decision authority and time.
eightd.problemBody: A precisely described problem is half solved. The standard structure is "Is / Is Not" (what occurs, what doesn't?) along the 5W2H questions (What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, How much). SIPOC, process maps and Voice-of-the-Customer collections help capture the problem objectively and verifiably — without premature blame and without hypotheses about the cause.
eightd.containmentBody: D3 protects the customer before the root cause is known. Typical containment actions: 100% inspection, sorting, quarantine of affected lots, replacement at the customer, additional incoming inspection. Crucially, containment is explicitly temporary and its effectiveness is monitored. It never replaces the permanent solution — it merely buys time for it.
eightd.rootcauseBody: D4 hunts the true causes — separately for the occurrence cause (why did the defect arise?), the escape cause (why wasn't it caught?) and the systemic cause (which gap in the management system allowed this?). 5-Why, Ishikawa, hypothesis tests and correlations validate suspicions rigorously. By the end of D4, causes are statistically or physically proven, not just plausible.
eightd.correctiveBody: With the cause known, the team plans Permanent Corrective Actions and picks the most effective option among alternatives. Evaluation criteria: effectiveness against the cause, freedom from risk (FMEA), effort, transferability to similar processes. Before rollout the effectiveness is verified — ideally via a designed experiment (DOE), a simulation or a limited pilot.
eightd.implementationBody: D6 rolls out the planned actions across the full scope and validates their effect in live operation. Control charts and capability analyses demonstrate that the problem no longer occurs. Once effectiveness is confirmed, the D3 containment actions are deliberately retired — the process now runs stably without crutches.
eightd.preventBody: D7 lifts the findings to the system level: which standards, specifications, work instructions, FMEAs, training plans and inspection routines must be updated so this problem cannot reappear anywhere — not in similar products or processes either? This is where the real learning leverage of 8D lies: a single defect becomes a permanent improvement to the management system.
eightd.recognizeBody: The closing step must never be skipped: make the success visible, formally discharge the team, document and communicate the lessons learned. Without this recognition, 8D processes lose internal acceptance — teams contribute less at the next incident if last time their effort vanished without comment. D8 is therefore not bureaucratic residue, but a central element of culture-building.
eightd.whenBody: 8D fits when a concrete defect has already occurred and needs reactive resolution — customer complaint, recurring production defect, audit finding, safety incident. Characteristic features: short time horizon (days to a few weeks), clear accountability to a recipient (customer, regulator), and the obligation to deliver solid documentation in the form of an 8D report. For proactive improvements without an acute trigger DMAIC remains the better choice; for greenfield development DMADV.
eightd.pitfall1: Treating D3 as the final solution. Sorting and 100% inspection are containment actions, not corrective actions — stopping here hides rather than solves the real problem.
eightd.pitfall2: Ending root-cause analysis at the first plausible explanation. Real 5-Why chains push at least to the systemic cause ("why does our process even allow this defect?") — anything shorter remains symptom treatment.
eightd.pitfall3: Forgetting D7. Implementing corrective actions only on the affected product without updating similar products / processes / FMEAs / work instructions guarantees that the same defect reappears six months later on a sister line.
eightd.pitfall4: Treating D8 as a chore. No thank-you, no communication of lessons learned, no visible value for the team — and at the next 8D call the most important people quietly opt out.
eightd.appBody: When you create a project with the "8D" cycle, the header shows eleven tiles (Data, D0…D8, More). Project Charter, SIPOC and VOC live in D2, Five-Why and Ishikawa in D4, DOE and Regression in D5, control charts in D6, FMEA in D7 and Lessons Learned in D8. Prepare (D0) and Containment (D3) currently lack dedicated modules — until those exist you can use the Todo list in D1/D3 to document entry checks and containment actions.

minitab.intro: Welcome to Qprovement! This page helps Minitab users get started. A lot will feel familiar — below we show where to find your usual features and how things are organised differently here.
minitab.conceptsIntro: Minitab works with a project that contains multiple worksheets. Qprovement follows a similar model but additionally organises work along the DMAIC phases (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control).
minitab.mappingIntro: The table below maps typical Minitab menu entries to their Qprovement equivalent.
minitab.row1c: Worksheets live in the central Data area and are not bound to any DMAIC phase — every analysis module can access every worksheet.
minitab.row2a: Stat → Basic Statistics → Display Descriptive Statistics
minitab.row2c: Results appear in the output panel next to the input.
minitab.row3c: Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk are computed automatically.
minitab.row4c: X̄-R, I-MR, p, np, c, u — all the Minitab standard charts are available.
minitab.row5b: Charts live inside the respective analysis modules
minitab.row5c: No separate Graph menu — charts are produced in context.
minitab.row6c: ANOVA is part of the Hypothesis Test module in the Analyze phase. Regression lives in the Improve phase, where it is typically used for model building.
minitab.row7c: Factorial designs, response surface and Plackett-Burman included.
minitab.row8c: Type-1 and Type-2 studies as standalone modules.
minitab.workflowIntro: While in Minitab you usually open a worksheet and launch analyses from the Stat menu, Qprovement is project-oriented:
minitab.workflow1: Create a new project at the top left (or open an existing one).
minitab.workflow2: Pick the DMAIC phase you want to work in (D, M, A, I, C).
minitab.workflow3: Add modules to that phase via the hamburger menu (☰) on the phase tile — each module is a tool (worksheet, chart, test, charter, …).
minitab.workflow4: Modules open as tabs in the workspace — similar to multiple worksheets in Minitab, but grouped by phase.
minitab.workflow5: Results are saved into the project automatically (local browser storage). Use the Export/Import buttons at the top to save projects as JSON.
minitab.dataBody: The worksheet module behaves like a Minitab worksheet: named columns, keyboard cell editing, copy/paste between Excel and the worksheet. CSV and XLSX import/export are available inside the module. Unlike Minitab, analysis modules pick their data source explicitly via a column picker — so you can always tell which data was used.
minitab.tip1: Session window: Qprovement has no classic session window. Each analysis appears in the output area of its module and stays there while the module is open.
minitab.tip2: Everything stays local: your projects and data are stored only in the browser (localStorage/IndexedDB) — there is no server and no cloud. That keeps them private, but it also means they can be lost if the browser cache is cleared, the profile is reset, or you switch to a different machine. Save your projects regularly via the Export button in the top header as a JSON file — you can restore them at any time through "Import".
minitab.tip3: Module help: as soon as a module is active, a question-mark icon appears in the top-right header — directly to the left of this training icon. Clicking it opens a module-specific guide with methodology, examples and common pitfalls. The icon is only visible when the active module has help content registered.
minitab.tip4: Validation: every statistical algorithm is validated against reference values (Minitab, R, NIST). The "Developing" area contains the Algorithm Lab with source code, formulas and test cases.

jmp.intro: Welcome to Qprovement! Coming from JMP, a lot will feel familiar — interactive charts, column roles, a central data-table model. This section shows where to find your usual analyses and what is deliberately organised differently here.
jmp.conceptsIntro: JMP is built around a data table and launches analyses from the Analyze and Graph menus. Qprovement also has central worksheets, but groups its tools along the DMAIC phases (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) rather than through a global analyse menu.
jmp.mappingIntro: The table below maps typical JMP menu entries to their Qprovement equivalent.
jmp.row1c: Worksheets live in the central Data area and are not bound to any DMAIC phase. Roles are not assigned globally but inside each analysis module.
jmp.row2c: The Distribution platform is split across several dedicated modules.
jmp.row3c: Which module applies depends — as in JMP — on the data types (continuous/categorical). ANOVA is part of the Hypothesis Test module.
jmp.row4a: Analyze → Quality and Process → Process Capability
jmp.row4c: Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk including a normality check.
jmp.row5a: Analyze → Quality and Process → Control Chart Builder
jmp.row5c: X̄-R, I-MR, p, np, c, u — with rule violations highlighted.
jmp.row6a: Analyze → Quality and Process → Measurement Systems Analysis
jmp.row6c: Type-1 and Type-2 studies as standalone modules.
jmp.row7c: Factorial designs, response surface and screening designs included.
jmp.row8b: Charts live inside the respective analysis modules
jmp.row8c: There is no free-form Graph Builder — charts are produced in the context of the module that analyses them.
jmp.workflowIntro: In JMP you open a data table and launch analyses from the menu. Qprovement is more project- and phase-oriented:
jmp.workflow1: Create a new project at the top left (or open an existing one).
jmp.workflow2: Pick the DMAIC phase you want to work in (D, M, A, I, C).
jmp.workflow3: Add modules to that phase via the hamburger menu (☰) on the phase tile — each module is a tool (worksheet, chart, test, charter, …).
jmp.workflow4: Analysis modules pick their data explicitly via a column picker from a worksheet — this is our counterpart to JMP's role assignment (X, Y, By, Freq, …).
jmp.workflow5: Results are saved into the project automatically (local browser storage). Use the Export/Import buttons at the top to save projects as JSON.
jmp.dataBody: The worksheet module plays the role of the JMP data table: named columns with types, keyboard cell editing, copy/paste from Excel. CSV and XLSX import/export are available inside the module. Column roles (X, Y, By, …) are not set on the worksheet itself but when you open an analysis module, via the column picker — so the same worksheet remains freely reusable across multiple analyses.
jmp.tip1: Interactive charts: charts in Qprovement support zoom, pan and tooltips, but they are not dynamically linked the way JMP "row state" connects views. Filtered views are produced by explicit selection inside the analysis module.
jmp.tip2: Everything stays local: your projects and data are stored only in the browser (localStorage/IndexedDB) — there is no server and no cloud. That keeps them private, but it also means they can be lost if the browser cache is cleared, the profile is reset, or you switch to a different machine. Save your projects regularly via the Export button in the top header as a JSON file — you can restore them at any time through "Import".
jmp.tip3: Module help: as soon as a module is active, a question-mark icon appears in the top-right header — directly to the left of this training icon. Clicking it opens a module-specific guide with methodology, examples and common pitfalls. The icon is only visible when the active module has help content registered.
jmp.tip4: JSL & scripting: Qprovement has no scripting language like JSL (yet). Reproducibility is achieved through the JSON export of the entire project — including every module state and worksheet.

triz.intro: TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving, Russian "Teoriya Resheniya Izobretatelskikh Zadach") is a systematic innovation methodology that the Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller developed from 1946 onwards by analysing hundreds of thousands of patents. While DMAIC improves existing processes, TRIZ helps resolve technical contradictions — situations where improving one property has so far inevitably worsened another.
triz.whyBody: Classical innovation tools such as brainstorming or trial-and-error rely on quantity — many ideas in the hope that one of them is good. TRIZ relies on pattern recognition instead: Altshuller showed that most inventive solutions stem from roughly 40 recurring principles, regardless of the field. Once you formulate a contradiction cleanly, you can look up historically proven solution paths instead of reinventing the wheel every time. Inventing turns from a flash of inspiration into a reproducible procedure.
triz.contradictionBody: A technical contradiction exists when improving one parameter degrades another (example: a car should become safer — i.e. heavier — but at the same time more fuel-efficient — i.e. lighter). A physical contradiction demands two opposite properties of the same element (hot and cold, hard and soft, present and absent). Inventive solutions resolve the contradiction rather than smoothing it over with a compromise.
triz.idealityBody: The Ideal Final Result (IFR) is a thought experiment: what if the desired function were delivered without a system, without cost and without harmful side-effects? TRIZ holds that technical systems evolve towards higher ideality — more benefit per cost, fewer parts, fewer harmful effects. The IFR sharpens the goal and prevents you from getting trapped inside the existing solution.
triz.evolutionBody: Altshuller identified eight laws by which technical systems evolve (e.g. increasing completeness, transition to the micro-level, dynamisation, self-adaptation). Rating your system's maturity against these laws reveals which evolutionary leaps are likely next — and which competing solutions will probably appear in the medium term.
triz.tool40Body: A library of 40 generic solution patterns (e.g. "Segmentation", "Prior action", "The other way round", "Phase transition"). Every principle is phrased abstractly and transfers across industries — from refrigerators to software architecture.
triz.toolMatrixBody: A 39×39 matrix that lists typical "improving" against "worsening" parameters. Each cell points to the statistically most frequent principles for that contradiction. The matrix shrinks the search space from "which of the 40 ideas applies?" down to "which 3–4 principles have proven useful for this exact constellation in the patent record?".
triz.tool9WindowsBody: A 3×3 grid that views the system on two axes simultaneously: hierarchy (subsystem · system · supersystem) and time (past · present · future). The tool breaks the tunnel-vision by deliberately forcing you into the neighbouring cell — opening up solution spaces that purely present-state thinking never reaches.
triz.toolArizTitle: ARIZ — Algorithm for Inventive Problem Solving
triz.toolArizBody: The heavyweight in the TRIZ toolbox: a nine-step algorithm that turns a vaguely formulated problem step-by-step into a physical contradiction and finally into its resolution. ARIZ is typically reserved for situations where the 40 principles and the contradiction matrix do not lead directly to a solution.
triz.whenTitle: When is TRIZ the right tool?
triz.whenBody: TRIZ shines whenever classical brainstorming or trial-and-error stall — typically with hard technical contradictions, in innovation and engineering work, or when an existing system has hit the limits of its architecture. For purely statistical process optimisation (reduce variation, raise Cpk), DMAIC remains the superior tool. TRIZ and DMAIC are not mutually exclusive: in the Improve phase of a DMAIC project, TRIZ can help when the identified root causes create what looks like an unavoidable trade-off.
triz.pitfall1: Giving up on the contradiction too early. If you don't formulate the trade-off cleanly, you fall back on a compromise ("a little more safety against a little more weight") and waste the chance for an inventive solution.
triz.pitfall2: Taking the 40 principles literally. They are abstract solution patterns, not finished blueprints — translating them onto your specific problem still requires thinking.
triz.pitfall3: Using TRIZ as a brainstorming add-on. Without a clean formulation of function, ideality and contradiction, TRIZ collapses into a list of buzzwords and loses its systematic edge.
triz.pitfall4: Watering down the Ideal Final Result during the real design. The strength of the IFR is precisely that it does not have to be reachable — it only points the direction. Making it "realistic" too early destroys exactly that orientation.
triz.appBody: Qprovement contains two TRIZ tools in the Improve phase: the "9 Windows" module for system analysis across hierarchy and time, and the "Contradiction Matrix" module with the 39 parameters and 40 principles after Altshuller. Both modules persist their state inside the project and can be JSON-exported and re-imported like any other module. You reach them via the hamburger menu (☰) on the Improve tile, or by drag-and-dropping them from the "More" tile into another phase if you want to use TRIZ already in the Define or Analyze step.

SeriesStats.name: Name of the series, as in the Series column and the legend: the column name, or the group value when grouped.
SeriesStats.stats: The figures of this series, each described individually. Empty for a series without values; the table then shows dashes.
SeriesStats.ci: The confidence intervals of this series at the chosen level, for mean, spread and variance. The table shows them after the value, as lower and upper bound. Empty if the series has fewer than two values or no spread. The table rounds the bounds to four decimals, magnitudes below 0.001 or from 10⁶ up to four significant digits.

Stats.n: Number of values in the series (N); the table shows it as a whole number.
Stats.mean: Mean x̄ = Σx / n, the sum of all values divided by their count. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.stddev: Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)), the sample spread with denominator n − 1 (column StdDev). The table rounds to four decimals. With only one value it is undefined: the table shows a dash, and in the agent result the value is empty.
Stats.variance: Variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1), the square of the standard deviation, with denominator n − 1. The table rounds to four decimals. With only one value it is undefined: the table shows a dash, and in the agent result the value is empty.
Stats.seMean: Standard error of the mean, s / √n. The table does not show it; it is what sets the width of the confidence interval for the mean. With only one value it is undefined; in the agent result the value is empty.
Stats.median: Median: the middle of the values sorted ascending, for an even count the mean of the two middle ones. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.min: Smallest value of the series. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.max: Largest value of the series. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.range: Range = largest minus smallest value. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.q1: First quartile: the limit below which a quarter of the sorted values lie, with linear interpolation between neighbouring values. The table does not show it.
Stats.q3: Third quartile: the limit below which three quarters of the sorted values lie, with linear interpolation between neighbouring values. The table does not show it.
Stats.skewness: Skewness g₁ = m₃ / m₂^1.5 with the central moments m₂ = Σ(x − x̄)² / n and m₃ = Σ(x − x̄)³ / n (denominator n, not corrected). Positive: the long tail is on the right, negative: on the left; 0 for symmetric values and for a series without spread. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.kurtosis: Kurtosis as excess: m₄ / m₂² − 3 with m₂ = Σ(x − x̄)² / n and m₄ = Σ(x − x̄)⁴ / n (denominator n, not corrected). 0 matches the normal distribution, positive means more peaked with heavy tails, negative flatter; 0 for a series without spread. The table rounds to four decimals.

StatsCi.mean: Confidence interval for the mean: x̄ ± t · s / √n with the t quantile at n − 1 degrees of freedom. Missing for fewer than two values or without spread.
StatsCi.variance: Confidence interval for the variance: from (n − 1)·s² / χ²(upper) to (n − 1)·s² / χ²(lower), with the χ² quantiles at n − 1 degrees of freedom. Missing for fewer than two values, without spread, or if a χ² quantile cannot be computed.
StatsCi.stddev: Confidence interval for the standard deviation: the square roots of the variance interval's bounds. Missing for fewer than two values, without spread, or if a χ² quantile cannot be computed.

saveAsModel.help: Saves the polynomial model (one or several X) in the project models, new or as an update of the model saved last; the button then reads “Update model”, and “Model saved” appears next to it. Without a model that can be saved nothing is stored.

predict.help: Predicts the response for the given values of the predictors and shows it under “Prediction”; the prediction stays empty when a predictor is left without a value or there is no result.

params.values: An object with one value per predictor id from predictors: a number, or one of the levels for categorical predictors. Missing predictors make the result null.

colRefs.help: The predictor columns X as { instanceId, sheetId, columnId }, in order.

yKey.help: The response column Y as key instanceId|sheetId|columnId, or null.

regType.help: The regression type, one of regTypes.

polyDegree.help: The polynomial degree (only used with the polynomial type).

activeDegrees.help: The degrees setParam('polyDegree') accepts now; a degree with too few paired rows for its term count is missing.

confLevel.help: The confidence level as a fraction (0.95).

alpha.help: The significance level α as a fraction (0.05).

excludedTerms.help: The term ids left out of the polynomial.

terms.help: The term ids setTerm accepts now; empty without a polynomial fit or aliasing.

experimentImports.help: The DoE responses importExperiment accepts, each { key, label }; the key is <planner instance id>|raw|<i> (|mean|, |lnvar| for mean and ln variance). The list is reloaded after the instance is added and on changes, and can still be empty right after module.add; importExperiment reads fresh itself and already accepts the key then.

activeImportSource.help: The DoE response the inputs came from, { experimentId, sourceColumn, transform }, or null. experimentId is the instance id of the DoE planner; when it or its experiment no longer exists, the entry stays and the module shows “no longer available”.

designNotice.help: Notes on the term set of an experimental design, each figure described individually under keys; null without a term set from an experimental design.

perXKeys.help: The single-X models setActiveX accepts; empty for the polynomial type and without result.

activeXKey.help: The single-X model result shows, or null.

pickableColumns.help: Per slot (x, y) the columns setColumns and setColumn accept, each { key, name }; y leaves out the columns chosen as X.

result.help: The fitted regression model with coefficients and analysis of variance, each figure described individually under keys; null without X or Y or when the fit fails (errorMsg then gives the reason). coefficients[].term is the coefficient name: for a categorical term it carries the level (Material[B]), while terms, excludedTerms and setTerm use the term id without the level (Material).

errorMsg.help: The message of the last failed fit, '' without error.

predictors.help: The inputs of the fitted model, each { id, label, kind, levels? }; empty without result.

canSaveModel.help: true when saveAsModel would store a model now (polynomial type with one or several X, and a result).

savedModelId.help: The id of the model saved last in the project models, or null.

prediction.help: { yHat, piLow, piHigh } of the last prediction, null without one and without result; piLow and piHigh are null where the model gives no prediction interval.

Params.regType: The model form: polynomial (main effects, from degree 2 also squares and interactions, with one or several X), exponential (y = a · eᵇˣ), logarithmic (y = a + b·ln(x)) or power (y = a · xᵇ). The last three fit a separate single model per X and use only suitable rows: exponential y > 0, logarithmic x > 0, power x > 0 and y > 0. A change fits again.
Params.polyDegree: The polynomial degree, 1, 2 or 3, default 1: degree 1 takes only the main effects, degree 2 adds squares and interactions, degree 3 adds cubic terms and higher interactions. A degree can only be chosen when there are more paired rows than terms; otherwise it is locked and the hint below the selection gives the number needed. Only used with the polynomial regression type.
Params.confLevel: The confidence level as a fraction between 0 and 1, so 0.95 instead of 95; the input field shows it in percent. It sets the confidence limits of the coefficients, the confidence and prediction bands in the chart and the prediction interval. The default is the project confidence level; it is independent of the significance level, the two are set separately.
Params.alpha: The significance level α as a fraction between 0 and 1, so 0.05 instead of 5; the input field shows it in percent. It changes no number, only the colouring: rows of the ANOVA and coefficient tables with p < α count as significant, the p-value (F) tile is green below α and yellow below 2α. The default is 1 − the project confidence level; after that it is independent of the confidence level, the two are set separately.

Result.type: The model form actually fitted: polynomial for the polynomial type (with one or several X), otherwise exponential, logarithmic or power for the single-X model shown.
Result.equation: The model equation as text, as shown below the figures, with coefficients rounded to four decimals.
Result.n: Number of rows used: rows with finite values in all X and in Y; for exponential, logarithmic and power only the rows that meet the condition of the model form (y > 0 or x > 0).
Result.R2: Coefficient of determination R² = 1 − SSE/SST: the share of the variation in Y the model explains, from 0 to 1. The tile is green from 0.8 and yellow from 0.5, red below.
Result.adjR2: Adjusted coefficient of determination, tile Adj. R²: 1 − (1 − R²) · (n − 1)/(n − p) with p coefficients including the intercept. It drops when a term costs more degrees of freedom than it explains, so it suits comparing models. The tile takes the colour of R².
Result.R2pred: Predicted coefficient of determination, tile R²(pred): 1 − PRESS/SST, where PRESS is the sum of the squared leave-one-out residuals eᵢ/(1 − hᵢᵢ). It measures how well the model predicts new data; well below R² it points to overfitting. Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power; the tile is then missing as well.
Result.Se: Standard error of the regression, tile Std. Error: S = √MSE, the typical deviation of the observations from the model, in the units of Y.
Result.Fstat: F statistic of the overall model, F = MSR/MSE from the Regression row of the ANOVA table; 0 when MSE is 0. The tile shows two decimals.
Result.fPVal: p-value of the F test, tile p-value (F): the probability of an F at least this large if all coefficients except the intercept were 0, from the F distribution with the degrees of freedom of regression and residuals. Below α the model counts as significant and the tile is green, below 2α yellow. 1 when the model has no degree of freedom or MSE is 0.
Result.dw: Durbin-Watson statistic Σ(eᵢ − eᵢ₋₁)²/SSE over the residuals in data order, between 0 and 4: around 2 no autocorrelation, below 1.5 positive, above 2.5 negative. 0 when SSE is 0; the tile shows three decimals.
Result.coefficients: The coefficient table, one row per estimated coefficient: for the polynomial first Intercept, then the terms; for exponential and power a and b, for logarithmic Intercept and ln(x).
Result.excludedTerms: The terms left out of the polynomial, by hand or because of aliasing, each as term name without level.
Result.anova: The analysis of variance of the model with the rows Regression, one per term, Residuals and Total; the same numbers as in the ANOVA table. For exponential, logarithmic and power there are no term rows.

Coefficient.term: The coefficient name: Intercept, a column name or a square or interaction term. A categorical predictor gets one row per level, whose name carries the level; including and excluding uses the term name without level.
Coefficient.coeff: The estimated coefficient b. The Coefficient column also shows the confidence interval next to it, from the lower to the upper confidence limit.
Coefficient.se: Standard error of the coefficient, column Std. Error: √(MSE · ((XᵀX)⁻¹)ⱼⱼ). Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power.
Coefficient.t: t-value b / Std. Error, tested against 0 with the degrees of freedom of the residuals. Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power.
Coefficient.pval: Two-sided p-value of the t test of b = 0; below α the term counts as significant and the row is highlighted. Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power.
Coefficient.ciLow: Lower confidence limit b − t · Std. Error, with t the (1 + confidence level)/2 quantile of the t distribution with the degrees of freedom of the residuals. Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power.
Coefficient.ciHigh: Upper confidence limit b + t · Std. Error, with the same t as the lower limit. Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power.
Coefficient.vif: Variance inflation factor 1/(1 − R²ⱼ), with R²ⱼ from regressing the predictor on the other continuous predictors that still have a term in the model. Only main effects of continuous predictors have a value, and only with at least two continuous predictors; otherwise empty. If only one of them still has a term in the model, the value is exactly 1. Above 5 the cell turns yellow, above 10 red; if the value over all chosen predictors differs, it is shown next to it in parentheses.

Anova.regression: The Regression row: the variation SSR explained by the model, with the F test of the overall model; degrees of freedom equal to the number of coefficients, not counting the constant term (the intercept for polynomial and logarithmic, the prefactor a for exponential and power).
Anova.terms: One indented row per term. When the polynomial is fitted with term blocks, this is the Type III decomposition per term block: the sum of squares the block explains in addition to all others, with the F test of the block. Otherwise one row per coefficient with SS = t² · MSE and one degree of freedom. Empty for exponential, logarithmic and power.
Anova.error: The Residuals row: the unexplained variation SSE with n − p degrees of freedom and MSE = SSE/(n − p).
Anova.total: The Total row: the total variation SST = Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² with n − 1 degrees of freedom, the sum of Regression and Residuals.

AnovaRow.term: The term name; only the term rows carry it.
AnovaRow.ss: Sum of squares of the row, column SS: the variation this source explains, that is left over (Residuals) or that is present in total (Total).
AnovaRow.df: Degrees of freedom of the row, column DF.
AnovaRow.ms: Mean square of the row, column MS = SS/DF. Missing in the Total row.
AnovaRow.f: F value of the row, column F: MS of the row divided by MS of the residuals. Only in the Regression row and the term rows.
AnovaRow.p: p-value of the F test of the row, from the F distribution with the DF of the row and the DF of the residuals; below α the row is highlighted as significant. Only in the Regression row and the term rows; empty where no p-value can be computed.

DesignNotice.aliased: The terms the experimental design cannot separate from others and that were therefore excluded, each with the terms it is aliased with.
DesignNotice.saturated: The terms excluded because the model would otherwise be saturated, leaving no degree of freedom for the residuals.

AliasedTerm.with: The terms it is aliased with.

regression.name: Regression Analysis
regression.description: Polynomial regression (degree 1–3, interactions), Exponential, Logarithmic, Power
regression.importSourceMissing: The experimental design this model came from is no longer available.
regression.degreeDisabledHint: Degree {deg} requires more than {terms} data points (currently: {n}).
regression.tipR2: Proportion of variance in Y explained by the model. 0 = no explanatory power, 1 = perfect fit. Values ≥ 0.8 indicate a good model.
regression.tipAdjR2: Like R², but adjusted for the number of predictors. Decreases when unnecessary variables are added — better suited for model comparison.
regression.tipPredR2: Predicted R²: How well the model predicts new data (leave-one-out). A large gap to R² suggests overfitting.
regression.tipStdError: Standard error of the regression (S): Average distance of observations from the regression line. Smaller = better fit. In Y units.
regression.tipFStat: F-statistic: Tests whether the overall model is significant (all coefficients jointly ≠ 0). Larger values indicate a significant model.
regression.tipPValueF: p-value of the F-test: Probability of observing the F-statistic under H₀ (no relationship). p < α → model is significant.
regression.tipDurbinWatson: Durbin-Watson statistic (0–4): Tests for autocorrelation in residuals. ≈ 2 = no autocorrelation, < 1.5 = positive, > 2.5 = negative autocorrelation.
regression.errSelectBoth: Please select both X and Y columns.
regression.errMinData: At least 3 valid data pairs required (currently: {n}).
regression.errInsufficientDf: Too few data points for the chosen model complexity.
regression.designNoticeAliased: {term} is aliased with {with} and was excluded.
regression.designNoticeSaturated: The model would be saturated (no degrees of freedom for error). Excluded: {terms}. Add replicates or center points.
regression.errAliasedTerms: The model cannot be estimated: {term} is aliased with {with}.

response-optimization.name: Response Optimization
response-optimization.description: Combines several saved regression models and searches for the factor point with the highest joint desirability (Derringer-Suich, multi-start Nelder-Mead).
response-optimization.whenToUse: When several saved regression models (responses of one design) must be traded off: assigns each selected model a goal (maximise, minimise, hit a target) with limits and weight, then searches the factor box for the point with the highest composite desirability D (Derringer-Suich, multi-start Nelder-Mead). Needs at least one saved regression model in the project; the models themselves are created in the regression module.

read.help: Returns the target specifications per model, the optimisation id, the saved models as references (id and name), whether an optimisation can run and why not, the stored optimum and the last error. result is null while no optimisation has run in this module (optId is then null) and when the stored optimisation record is gone; it shows the last successful run, not necessarily the current specifications. errorMsg stays empty until a runOptimize run computes nothing.

params.options: Optional; this module holds no bulk data.

setSpec.help: Sets one target specification of a saved model: selected, kind (max, min, target), lower, upper, target or weight. Nothing is computed; canOptimize and diagnosticReasons update, the stored result stays until runOptimize runs. Refuses a modelId that is not in selectableModels, an unknown key and a value that does not fit the key.

params.modelId: The id of a model from selectableModels. Any other value is an error.
params.key: Which option; each is described individually under keys. Any other value is an error.
params.value: The value; type and allowed range per key are given under keys.

runOptimize.help: Optimises the selected models together and stores the optimum in the project; it appears under “Result”. If optimisation is blocked (no model selected, R²adj too low, significant lack of fit or different factors across the selected models) nothing is computed, the previous result stays and a message above the button names the reasons. If the computation fails, the result also stays as it was and the message names the error. After a successful run the message disappears.

specs.help: The settings per response, each described under keys.

optId.help: The id of the stored optimisation; null before the first successful runOptimize.

selectableModels.help: The saved models of the project as references { id, name } - no coefficients; read a model in the regression module that created it. Empty while the project has no saved model. These ids are what setSpec accepts as modelId.

canOptimize.help: True only if at least one model is selected and diagnosticReasons is empty; otherwise runOptimize computes nothing.

diagnosticReasons.help: The reasons that block the optimisation, as texts: R²adj below 0.5, significant lack of fit (p below 0.05) or a different factor structure among the selected models. Empty when nothing blocks, and also empty while no model is selected (optimisation is still blocked then).

result.help: The stored optimum, each figure described individually under keys; null until an optimization has run or when the stored data set is missing.

errorMsg.help: Why the last runOptimize computed nothing: the blocking reasons joined by '; ', 'No model selected.' or the engine error. Empty before the first runOptimize and after a successful run; cleared again as soon as the model list, the selection or a target specification changes.

Spec.selected: Whether this model (this response) takes part in the optimisation; the checkbox in the model header. Only included models show their desirability function and contribute to the composite desirability D; initially none is included. Optimising is possible only when at least one model is included and no diagnosis blocks (R²adj below 0.5, significant lack of fit with p below 0.05, or different factors among the selected models).
Spec.kind: The desirability function of the response: Maximise, Minimise or Target value, default Maximise. Maximise: d = 0 for y ≤ Lower, d = (y − Lower) / (Upper − Lower) in between, d = 1 for y ≥ Upper. Minimise mirrors it: d = 1 up to Lower, d = (Upper − y) / (Upper − Lower) in between, d = 0 from Upper on. Target value: d = 1 exactly at the target, falling linearly to 0 towards Lower and Upper, 0 at and beyond the limits. The shape is always linear (exponent 1). If Upper is not above Lower, d jumps straight between 0 and 1 for Maximise and Minimise; for Target value d is then always 0.
Spec.lower: The lower limit of the desirability function in the unit of the response: for Maximise d = 0 here, for Minimise d = 1, for Target value d = 0. The default is the smallest measured value in the model data (0 without data). A finite number; whether it lies below Upper is not checked.
Spec.upper: The upper limit of the desirability function in the unit of the response: for Maximise d = 1 here, for Minimise d = 0, for Target value d = 0. The default is the largest measured value in the model data (1 without data). A finite number; whether it lies above Lower is not checked.
Spec.target: The target at which the desirability function reaches d = 1. Effective only for the Target value function and shown only then; for Maximise and Minimise it stays stored but has no effect. The default is the midpoint between the smallest and largest measured value, 0.5 without measured values. A finite number; whether it lies between Lower and Upper is not checked.
Spec.weight: The weight w of this response in the composite desirability D = (Π dᵢ^wᵢ)^(1/Σwᵢ): a response with weight 2 counts twice as much as one with weight 1. A number greater than 0, default 1.

Result.xOpt: The factor settings of the optimum, one per factor in the order of the factor names: continuous factors as a number (column Value, four decimals), categorical ones as the level name. The search runs inside the box of factor limits of the first selected model (−1 to 1 if none are given) with Nelder-Mead from 8 random starting points (seed 42, at most 400 iterations per start); the start with the highest D wins. With categorical factors every level combination is searched this way on its own and the best one is taken.
Result.yPredictions: The predicted response values at the optimum, each computed from its model’s regression equation, in the order of the model names (column Prediction, four decimals).
Result.dPerResponse: The individual desirability d per response at the optimum, between 0 and 1: the model’s desirability function applied to its prediction (column d, three decimals). 1 means the specification is fully met, 0 means unacceptable.
Result.D: The composite desirability at the optimum, the weighted geometric mean of the individual desirabilities: D = (Π dᵢ^wᵢ)^(1/Σwᵢ) with the weights wᵢ. If any d is 0, D = 0. The tile shows D with three decimals, green from 0.8, yellow from 0.5, red below. D belongs to the last optimisation run: if a specification is changed afterwards, the result is current again only after optimising anew.
Result.ciAtOpt: Confidence interval of the predictions at the optimum; not computed yet and always empty.
Result.paretoFront: Pareto front of the responses; not computed yet and always empty.
Result.factorNames: The factor names from the first selected model, in the same order as the factor settings (column Factor).
Result.modelNames: The names of the included models (responses), in the same order as the predictions and individual desirabilities (column Model).
Result.iter: The number of Nelder-Mead iterations: without categorical factors those of the best of the 8 starts, with categorical factors the sum over all level combinations.

response-optimization.emptyState: No saved models yet. Save a regression model from the Regression module first.
response-optimization.placeholderResult: No optimum computed yet. Select a model, set the desirability spec, then optimise.
response-optimization.lowR2: Model "{name}" has R²adj = {value}, which is below the minimum required for a meaningful optimisation.
response-optimization.factorMismatch: Model "{name}" has a different factor structure than the other selected models.
response-optimization.lackOfFit: Model "{name}" has a significant lack of fit (p = {value}). The polynomial form does not match the data — refit before optimising.
response-optimization.tipD: Composite desirability D — geometric mean of all individual desirabilities

glm-regression.whenToUse: When a response is attributive — good/bad, yes/no, proportions — or a count (defects, complaints), and its relationship with predictors is to be modelled: binary logistic, Poisson or negative binomial, detected automatically on request.

read.help: Returns the inputs (X, Y, trials column, method, confidence, α, cutoff), the sets the actions accept now, and the fit as numbers in result (null without a shown fit or after a failed fit; errorMsg then names the reason). If Y or X is cleared, the result is discarded: result is then null.

setColumns.help: The data collection columns that supply this role; after a change the analysis is recomputed. The order is kept, columns chosen twice count once and text columns become categorical predictors; if the response or the trials column is among the new predictors, it is cleared.

params.slot: One of activeMultiSlots; this module only has 'x'.
params.refs: List of column references { instanceId, sheetId, columnId } from pickableColumns.x, in order; [] clears X.

setColumn.help: The data collection column that supplies this role; after a change the analysis is recomputed. For grouped data a second column supplies the number of trials; the response is then read as a proportion.

params.ref: Column reference { instanceId, sheetId, columnId } from pickableColumns.y (columns not chosen as X) or pickableColumns.trials (additionally without Y), or null to clear.

setParam.help: Sets the method, the confidence level, α or the classification cutoff. method, confLevel and alpha fit again; cutoff only recomputes classification.

params.key: Which option; each is described individually under keys, the ones allowed in the current state are listed in activeParams. Any other value is an error.
params.value: The value; type and allowed range per key are given under keys. confLevel and alpha as a fraction; the other becomes 1 minus this value.

swapSuccess.help: For a binary response swaps which level counts as success and fits again; the coefficients change sign and the odds ratios become their reciprocals. Without a binary result nothing happens.

autoRun.help: Fits when X and Y are set; otherwise an earlier result is discarded.

runAnalysis.help: Fits now. Without X, without Y or with fewer than three rows the result is discarded and errorMsg names the reason.

saveAsModel.help: Saves the displayed fit to the project models, new or as an update of the model saved last, so that other tools can use it. Without a converged fit or without values of the response nothing is saved.

predict.help: Computes the predicted response with confidence limits for the entered term values, as a probability for binomial and as an expected count for Poisson and negative binomial. The limits are missing when the fit does not carry them; if a term is left without a value or there is no result, there is no prediction.

params.values: An object with one number per term from predictionTerms; categorical predictors as 0/1 per dummy term. Missing terms leave the result null.

colRefs.help: The predictor columns X as column references, in order.

yKey.help: The response column as key instanceId|sheetId|columnId, or null.

trialsKey.help: The column with the number of trials per row (grouped binomial data), or null.

method.help: The chosen method: one of methods; 'auto' detects the family from the response.

methods.help: All methods setParam accepts for method.

confLevel.help: Confidence level as a fraction; alpha is 1 minus this value.

alpha.help: Significance level as a fraction; confLevel is 1 minus this value.

cutoff.help: Classification threshold for a binomial fit, from 0 to 1.

successClass.help: For a binary response the level counted as success (1) and the other one as failure; the button next to it swaps them. Empty without a binary response.

pickableColumns.help: Per slot (x, y, trials) the columns setColumns/setColumn accept, each { key, name }.

result.help: The fitted generalized linear model, each figure described individually under keys; null without a displayed fit.

classification.help: The confusion table at the cutoff, each figure described individually under keys; null without a binomial result.

errorMsg.help: The message of the last failed fit, '' without error.

predictionTerms.help: The terms a prediction takes, in model order (dummies and interactions included); [] without a shown fit.

savedModelId.help: Id of the model saved last in the project models, or null.

prediction.help: The last prediction as numbers (linear, response, ciLower, ciUpper), or null without a prediction, after a new fit or without a shown result.

Params.method: The distribution family, section Method: auto-detection, binomial (logistic regression with logit link), Poisson or negative binomial (both with log link). Auto-detection picks binomial when the response has exactly two levels; for non-negative integers negative binomial when variance/mean exceeds 2, otherwise Poisson; proportions between 0 and 1 are fitted binomially but need a column with the number of trials. A change recomputes.
Params.confLevel: The confidence level as a fraction between 0 and 1, so 0.95 rather than 95; the input shows it in percent. It sets the confidence limits of the coefficients, the ratios and the prediction. The significance level becomes 1 minus this value. A change recomputes.
Params.alpha: The significance level α as a fraction between 0 and 1, so 0.05 rather than 5; the input shows it in percent. The confidence level becomes 1 minus this value, and the confidence limits change accordingly. A change recomputes.
Params.cutoff: The classification cutoff between 0 and 1, default 0.5, set with the slider on the ROC / Classification tab: an observation counts as predicted 1 when its estimated probability reaches at least the cutoff. A new value only recounts the confusion table and its rates; the model is not refitted. Only available with a binomial result.

Result.family: The family actually fitted, with link function and, for negative binomial, the estimated θ; with auto-detection the family it chose.
Result.quasi: Whether quasi-Poisson is active: if the Poisson fit shows χ²/df above 1.5, it is refitted with the dispersion φ = Pearson χ²/df; the coefficients stay, standard errors and confidence intervals are widened by √φ, and a warning gives φ.
Result.autoReason: The reason for the automatic choice. It appears as a hint below the method while “Auto-Detect (recommended)” is chosen; the result holds the key of that hint text. Possible reasons: exactly two levels, count data, overdispersed count data, proportions without trials, or non-negative values as the fallback. Empty when a method is chosen explicitly.
Result.n: Number of rows used, row n: rows with finite values in Y, all X and, where given, the trials.
Result.iterations: Number of IRLS iterations until convergence, row IRLS Iterations; a high count points to a difficult fit such as separation.
Result.aic: Akaike information criterion, tile AIC: −2ℓ + 2k with the log-likelihood ℓ and k parameters (coefficients, plus θ for negative binomial). Smaller is better; only for comparing models of the same response.
Result.bic: Bayesian information criterion, tile BIC: −2ℓ + ln(n) · k; penalises extra parameters more than AIC. Smaller is better.
Result.deviance: Residual deviance: twice the log-likelihood gap to the saturated model. Compared with the null deviance it shows how much the predictors explain.
Result.nullDeviance: Null deviance: the deviance of the intercept-only model, the reference for residual deviance and pseudo-R².
Result.logLikelihood: The maximised log-likelihood ℓ of the model; the basis of AIC, BIC and the pseudo-R².
Result.pseudoR2: The three pseudo coefficients of determination McFadden, Nagelkerke and Cox-Snell, which compare the model's log-likelihood with that of the intercept-only model.
Result.coefficients: The coefficient table, one row per term, Intercept first, then the predictors; a categorical predictor gets one dummy row per level.
Result.auc: Area under the ROC curve, tile AUC, between 0 and 1: 0.5 is guessing, 1 a perfect separation. The tile is green from 0.8, yellow from 0.6, red below. Only with a binomial result, otherwise empty.
Result.hosmerLemeshow: Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test: the observations are split into 10 groups by estimated probability (fewer with little data, at least 4) and observed and expected events are compared by χ² with groups − 2 degrees of freedom; a small p-value speaks against the fit. With fewer than 20 observations (trials for grouped data) the test is skipped and then shows statistic 0 and p = 1. Only with a binomial result, otherwise empty.
Result.overdispersionRatio: χ²/df (Overdispersion): Pearson χ² divided by n − p; the same value as the ratio of the overdispersion check. Above 1.5 the Poisson fit counts as overdispersed. Only for Poisson, otherwise empty.
Result.overdispersion: The overdispersion check on the Diagnostics tab with Pearson χ², degrees of freedom and their ratio. Only for Poisson, otherwise empty.
Result.vif: Variance inflation factors of the predictors, table VIF, same order as vifTerms; the first value belongs to the first predictor after the intercept, i.e. the second row of the coefficient table. Above 5 the cell is marked, above 10 a warning is shown. Only with two or more predictor columns, otherwise empty; a single value is empty when it cannot be computed.
Result.vifTerms: The terms belonging to the values in vif, same order, column “Term” of the VIF table: the predictors after the intercept, i.e. the coefficient terms from the second row on. Empty when no VIF table appears.
Result.warnings: The warnings above the output, for example on separation, few events, slow convergence, overdispersion or quasi-Poisson. The texts are in the language of the interface.
Result.warningDetails: The warnings as a code with the inserted numbers, in the same order as warnings; the code is the text key, for example warnFewEvents with epv.
Result.equation: The model equation as text, as shown under Model Equation: logit(p) for binomial, log(μ) for Poisson and negative binomial, equal to the intercept plus coefficient times term, rounded to four decimals.

Warning.code: The id of the warning, equal to the text key.
Warning.values: The numbers behind the notice, by name, unrounded; shares as a value between 0 and 1; not computable is null.

Family.name: The distribution family: binomial, poisson or negbin; the row Family shows the translated name.
Family.link: The link function that connects the expected value to the linear predictor: logit for binomial, log for Poisson and negative binomial.
Family.theta: The estimated shape parameter θ, row θ (dispersion), of the negative binomial distribution, variance = μ + μ²/θ; a small θ means strong overdispersion. Only for negative binomial, otherwise empty.

PseudoR2.mcfadden: McFadden R², tile McFadden R²: 1 − ℓ/ℓ₀ with the log-likelihood ℓ of the model and ℓ₀ of the intercept-only model. The tile is green from 0.4, yellow from 0.2, red below; values from 0.2 to 0.4 already count as a good fit.
PseudoR2.nagelkerke: Nagelkerke R², tile Nagelkerke R²: the Cox-Snell R² divided by its largest possible value 1 − exp(2ℓ₀/n), so that it reaches 1. The tile is green from 0.8, yellow from 0.5, red below.
PseudoR2.coxSnell: Cox-Snell R²: 1 − exp(−2/n · (ℓ − ℓ₀)); does not always reach 1 even for a perfect fit.

GlmCoefficient.term: The term name: Intercept, a column name, or for categorical predictors one dummy term per level.
GlmCoefficient.estimate: The estimated coefficient b on the link scale (logit or log). The Coefficient column also shows the confidence interval next to it, from the lower to the upper limit.
GlmCoefficient.se: Standard error of the coefficient, column SE, from the inverse Fisher information; widened by √φ under quasi-Poisson.
GlmCoefficient.z: Wald z, column z: the coefficient divided by its standard error.
GlmCoefficient.p: Two-sided p-value of the Wald test of b = 0, 2 · (1 − Φ(|z|)); below α the term counts as significant and is highlighted.
GlmCoefficient.ciLower: Lower confidence limit b − z · SE, with z the (1 + confidence level)/2 quantile of the normal distribution.
GlmCoefficient.ciUpper: Upper confidence limit b + z · SE, with the same z as the lower limit.
GlmCoefficient.ratio: The ratio exp(b) with confidence limits, column OR for binomial (odds ratio) or RR for Poisson and negative binomial (rate ratio): the factor by which the odds or the rate change per unit of the predictor. Empty for the intercept.

Ratio.value: The ratio exp(b): odds ratio for binomial, rate ratio for Poisson and negative binomial; 1 means no effect.
Ratio.lower: Lower limit of the ratio, exp of the coefficient's lower confidence limit.
Ratio.upper: Upper limit of the ratio, exp of the coefficient's upper confidence limit.

HosmerLemeshow.statistic: The χ² statistic of the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, the sum over the groups of (observed − expected)² divided by the expected variance; 0 when the test was skipped.
HosmerLemeshow.pValue: p-value of the Hosmer-Lemeshow test from the χ² distribution with groups − 2 degrees of freedom; below α it speaks against the fit. 1 when the test was skipped.

Overdispersion.pearsonChi2: Pearson χ²: the sum of the squared Pearson residuals of the Poisson fit, row Pearson χ².
Overdispersion.df: Degrees of freedom, row df: n − p, the number of observations minus the number of coefficients.
Overdispersion.ratio: The ratio χ²/df; under Poisson it should be close to 1.
Overdispersion.overdispersed: Whether overdispersion is detected: true when χ²/df is above 1.5; the hint towards negative binomial regression then appears and quasi-Poisson becomes active. Above 3 the computation counts it as severe, but that is not shown separately.

Classification.cutoff: The cutoff of the confusion table: predicted 1 when the estimated probability reaches at least the cutoff, otherwise predicted 0.
Classification.tp: True positives: actual 1 and predicted 1; for grouped data the trials are counted.
Classification.fn: False negatives: actual 1 but predicted 0; for grouped data the trials are counted.
Classification.fp: False positives: actual 0 but predicted 1; for grouped data the trials are counted.
Classification.tn: True negatives: actual 0 and predicted 0; for grouped data the trials are counted.
Classification.sensitivity: Sensitivity: true positives / (true positives + false negatives), the share of actual ones that are detected; 0 when there are none.
Classification.specificity: Specificity: true negatives / (true negatives + false positives), the share of actual zeros that are detected; 0 when there are none.
Classification.accuracy: Accuracy: (true positives + true negatives) / all, the share of correctly classified observations.
Classification.precision: Precision: true positives / (true positives + false positives), the share of real ones among those predicted as 1; 0 when nothing is predicted as 1.

glm-regression.name: Regression (Attributive)
glm-regression.description: Binary logistic, Poisson, and negative binomial regression for attributive/count data
glm-regression.autoDetectBinary: Response has exactly 2 values → binary logistic regression recommended.
glm-regression.autoDetectPoisson: Response is non-negative integer (count data) → Poisson regression recommended.
glm-regression.autoDetectNegbin: Response is count data with overdispersion (variance > mean) → negative binomial regression recommended.
glm-regression.autoDetectProportion: Response contains proportions (0–1) → binary logistic regression recommended.
glm-regression.autoDetectProportionAmbiguous: Response contains proportions in [0, 1]. Grouped binomial regression requires a trials column per observation; without it the likelihood is ill-defined.
glm-regression.autoDetectDefault: Response is non-negative → Poisson regression used as default.

glm-regression.warnSmallN: Small sample relative to number of parameters (n/p < 10). Results may be unreliable.
glm-regression.warnFewEvents: Few events per predictor (EPV = {epv} < 10). Coefficients and p-values may be biased.
glm-regression.warnSlowConverge: Model required many iterations to converge — may indicate poor conditioning.
glm-regression.warnOverdispersion: Overdispersion detected in Poisson model. Consider switching to negative binomial.
glm-regression.warnQuasiActivated: Quasi-Poisson active (φ = {phi}). Standard errors and confidence intervals were scaled by √φ.
glm-regression.warnSeparationStrong: Complete or quasi-complete separation detected. Coefficients and standard errors are unreliable — drop the separating predictor or merge classes.
glm-regression.warnThetaUnstable: θ estimate did not converge (θ = {theta}). Data are likely near-Poisson — switch the method to Poisson, or fix θ manually.
